title: Numbers, days and dates
topic: numbers from 0 to 100; days, months, dates; prices and age
why: After telling the time, this lesson covers all the numbers up to 100, including the famous soixante-dix and quatre-vingts, then days, months, dates and prices. You can now give your age, a date, a phone number and understand what you pay at the market.

{"lessons": ["

From 0 to 69

Up to 69, French numbers are fairly logical. Learn the first sixteen by heart; after that, it's tens plus units.

0 zéro1 un2 deux3 trois
4 quatre5 cinq6 six7 sept
8 huit9 neuf10 dix11 onze
12 douze13 treize14 quatorze15 quinze
16 seize17 dix-sept18 dix-huit19 dix-neuf
20 vingt30 trente40 quarante50 cinquante

60 is soixante. Between the tens, use a hyphen: vingt-deux, trente-cinq, quarante-huit. But with 1, it's et un, with no hyphen: vingt et un, trente et un, soixante et un. Before a feminine noun, un becomes une: vingt et une heures.

Six, dix, huit: three sounds

These numbers change their ending depending on what follows:

  • alone, the final consonant is heard: six (“sees”), dix (“dees”), huit (“weet”);
  • before a consonant, it's silent: six livres (“see”), dix stylos, huit jours;
  • before a vowel, liaison: six‿euros and dix‿euros with a “z”, huit‿euros with a “t”.

Also watch cinq (the q is heard: “sank”), sept (the p is silent: “set”) and vingt (the g and t are silent, but the t comes back in vingt-deux…vingt-neuf).

Age still takes avoir: Elle a dix-sept ans. And now you can say any age up to 100!

", "

70 to 100: French arithmetic

Here France does something surprising. There is no single word for 70, 80 or 90: you count with sixty and twenty.

numberFrenchliterally
70soixante-dixsixty-ten
71soixante et onzesixty and eleven
72soixante-douzesixty-twelve
79soixante-dix-neufsixty-ten-nine
80quatre-vingtsfour twenties
81quatre-vingt-unfour-twenty-one (no et)
90quatre-vingt-dixfour-twenty-ten
99quatre-vingt-dix-neuffour-twenty-ten-nine
100centa hundred (no un)

Three spelling details: soixante et onze keeps the et, but quatre-vingt-un and quatre-vingt-onze don't; quatre-vingts takes an -s only when no other number follows it (quatre-vingts ans, but quatre-vingt-deux); and 100 is simply cent, never “un cent”.

Mamie Jeanne a quatre-vingt-deux ans.Grandma Jeanne is eighty-two.

In Belgium and Switzerland, people say septante (70) and nonante (90), and in parts of Switzerland huitante (80). Good to recognize, but in France, and in your answers, always use the French system.

Phone numbers

A French phone number has ten digits, written and read in pairs: 06 12 34 56 78 = zéro six, douze, trente-quatre, cinquante-six, soixante-dix-huit. Mobile numbers start with 06 or 07.

To think fast: for 70 to 79, say soixante + 10 to 19; for 90 to 99, quatre-vingt + 10 to 19.

", "

Days, months, dates and prices

Days and months are masculine and, unlike English, written in lowercase: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche; janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre.

With a day, the article changes the meaning: lundi alone = this Monday; le lundi = on Mondays, every Monday.

Lundi, je travaille. Le samedi, je ne travaille pas.This Monday, I'm working. On Saturdays, I don't work.

The date

French uses le + number + month, with no “of” and no “-th”: le 14 juillet, le 3 mai. Only the 1st is different: le premier mai (written le 1er mai). To give today's date: Nous sommes le 3 mai. or On est le 3 mai. In writing, the day comes first: 03/05 is May 3rd.

Prices

To ask: Ça coûte combien ? or simply C'est combien ? To give the total: Ça fait… French uses a comma as the decimal point, and the € sign after the number, with a space: 12,50 €, read douze euros cinquante. One euro has a hundred centimes.

C'est combien, le livre ? — Ça fait quinze euros quatre-vingt-dix.How much is the book? — That's fifteen euros ninety.

coûter (to cost) is a regular -er verb: le livre coûte dix euros, les livres coûtent vingt euros.
